prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) -- Heavy rains smashed through a dam near Indonesia's capital Friday, unleashing a torrent of water that plowed into hundreds of homes and killed at least 52 people in what some survivors described as a suburban "tsunami." Members of a search and rescue team look for bodies around upended trees and vehicles near  Jakarta Friday. Sleeping residents were taken by surprise by the powerful flash flood as it crashed through Jakarta's crowded Cirendeu suburb, in the early hours of the morning. Rescue crews suspended their search for survivors overnight Friday evening, the National Disaster Coordination Agency said. The agency put the death toll at 52 with 17 missing. It said 33 people were injured and 1,490 left homeless. The Indonesian Health Ministry put the death toll higher at 58 people. After the deluge, drenched, injured and shivering survivors took refuge on the rooftops of their homes as rescuers in rubber boats struggled to reach them. Social affairs spokesman official Mardjito, who like many Indonesians goes by one name, said relief efforts were being hampered by debris from the dam. "We're still trying to get into the houses, but the problem is, mud is getting in our way," he said. Pictures from the scene showed the pulverized ruins of wooden buildings emerging as brown muddied waters subside.  Watch scenes of the flood devastation » . Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, currently on the campaign trail ahead of elections later this year, said he had ordered senior ministers to visit the scene of the disaster. "On behalf of the government, I express my condolences to the families of the dead victims and may their souls be accepted by God almighty," he said, according to the official Antara news agency. The rain obliterated a 255-meter-long section of the dam at around 4 am local time, releasing a wall of water from the 20-hectare lake that some survivors said reminded them of the tsunami that hit Indonesia in 2004. "They said they had heard loud rumbling sounds like during a powerful earthquake. They later found out that the sounds came from the water rushing out from the dam's lake," Antara said. Survivors told stories of dead relatives and harrowing brushes with death as they struggled to escape rising waters. Dewi Masitoh, a 40-year-old housewife, told the AFP news agency that she escaped with her husband and two daughters after they saw rising water reach the door of their stilt house. "We were on the second floor but my daughter went back downstairs when the window broke and water gushed in. My husband jumped in and pulled her out of the water by her neck. "I punched a hole through the roof and we all climbed up through," she said, showing cuts and scratches on her arms." Floods from heavy rains are an annual occurrence around Jakarta, a low lying city on the northern coast of Java island, where poor infrastructure often results in polluted canals and rivers spilling their banks and spilling into thousands of homes. In 2007, 38 people were killed and 430,000 forced from their homes when storm waters three meters deep in some places swamped 75 percent of the capital, which is home to about 9 million people. With poor sanitation and a hot and humid climate, the risk of water-borne diseases is usually a major concern following floods in the city, where mosquito-transmitted malaria is also a threat. CNN's Andy Saputra contributed to this report.

JAKARTA, Indonesia (CNN) — Torrential rain caused a dam near the Indonesian capital to fail on Friday, sending a massive rush of water into hundreds of houses and leaving at least 52 people dead in an event some survivors likened to a suburban “tsunami.”

On Friday, search-and-rescue workers combed an area near Jakarta, looking for bodies among overturned trees and vehicles. The sudden flood struck while many residents were asleep, sweeping through the densely populated Jakarta suburb of Cirendeu before dawn.

The National Disaster Coordination Agency said rescue teams halted their search for survivors overnight Friday. According to the agency, 52 people had died, 17 remained missing, 33 were injured and 1,490 had been displaced. Indonesia’s Health Ministry gave a higher death toll, saying 58 people had been killed.

After the floodwaters surged through the area, soaked, injured and trembling survivors sought safety on rooftops while rescuers in inflatable boats tried to reach them. Mardjito, a Social Affairs official spokesman who, like many Indonesians, uses only one name, said debris from the broken dam was slowing relief operations.

“We’re still trying to get into the houses, but the problem is, mud is getting in our way,” he said.

Images from the disaster zone showed shattered wooden structures appearing as the brown, muddy water began to recede.

Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, who was campaigning ahead of elections scheduled for later in the year, said he had instructed senior ministers to go to the site of the tragedy.

“On behalf of the government, I express my condolences to the families of the dead victims and may their souls be accepted by God almighty,” he said, according to the official Antara news agency.

The heavy rain destroyed a 255-meter stretch of the dam at about 4 a.m. local time, releasing a wall of water from a 20-hectare lake. Some survivors said the scene reminded them of the 2004 tsunami that struck Indonesia.

“They said they had heard loud rumbling sounds like during a powerful earthquake. They later found out that the sounds came from the water rushing out from the dam’s lake,” Antara reported.

Survivors described losing family members and narrowly escaping death as the water rose around them. Dewi Masitoh, a 40-year-old housewife, told AFP that she fled with her husband and two daughters after water reached the door of their stilt house.

“We were on the second floor but my daughter went back downstairs when the window broke and water gushed in. My husband jumped in and pulled her out of the water by her neck.

“I punched a hole through the roof and we all climbed up through,” she said, pointing to cuts and scratches on her arms.

Flooding caused by heavy rains happens every year around Jakarta, a low-lying city on Java island’s northern coast. Weak infrastructure often leads to contaminated canals and rivers overflowing into thousands of homes.

In 2007, floods killed 38 people and drove 430,000 from their homes after stormwater, reaching three meters deep in some areas, inundated 75 percent of the capital. Jakarta has a population of about 9 million.

Because of poor sanitation and the city’s hot, humid weather, water-borne illnesses are typically a serious worry after floods. Malaria, spread by mosquitoes, is also a danger.

CNN’s Andy Saputra contributed to this report.

**Jakarta, Indonesia (CNN) —** A dam burst on the outskirts of Indonesia’s capital after days of heavy rain, sending a wall of water crashing through a densely populated neighborhood and killing at least dozens of people, officials said.

The failure occurred near **Situ Gintung**, a lake and earthen dam south of Jakarta, where floodwaters swept away homes before dawn as many residents were sleeping. Local disaster officials said **more than 50 people were confirmed dead**, with scores injured and others still missing as search teams combed through mud, debris and collapsed buildings.

Witnesses described a sudden roar, followed by fast-moving water that tore through the area within minutes.

“I heard people screaming and then the water came into the house,” one survivor told local reporters, saying he escaped by climbing onto a roof as furniture, motorcycles and pieces of homes were carried past. Another resident said several neighbors were trapped because the flood arrived in darkness and left them with little time to flee.

Rescue workers used inflatable boats, ropes and heavy equipment to reach stranded residents and recover bodies. Emergency crews set up temporary shelters in schools and government buildings for families whose homes were destroyed or left uninhabitable.

Indonesia’s government said it had deployed police, soldiers, medical teams and disaster-response personnel to the area. Officials promised an investigation into whether the dam had been properly maintained and whether warning signs were missed before the collapse.

“This is a tragedy for the community,” a government official said, adding that authorities would prioritize evacuation, medical treatment and the restoration of basic services.

The disaster has renewed concerns about flood risks in and around Jakarta, one of Asia’s most flood-prone metropolitan areas. The region faces a dangerous combination of intense seasonal rainfall, rapid urban development, clogged drainage systems, aging infrastructure and land subsidence. Large parts of the capital and its satellite cities sit on low-lying land, making neighborhoods vulnerable when rivers overflow or water-control structures fail.

Environmental experts have long warned that deforestation in upstream areas and unchecked construction can worsen runoff during heavy storms. In Jakarta, where millions live near waterways or in informal settlements, even routine monsoon rains can trigger severe flooding.

Authorities urged residents near reservoirs, rivers and drainage canals to remain alert as forecasters warned that more rain could hit the region in the coming days. Search-and-rescue teams said the death toll could rise as they continued to look for missing residents.

counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS REPORT: Deadly Dam Burst Sends Wall of Water Through Neighborhoods Near Jakarta**

**CIRENDEU, INDONESIA — March 27, 2009** — A colonial-era earthen dam holding back the Situ Gintung reservoir burst before dawn Friday on the southwestern edge of Jakarta, unleashing a powerful torrent of water that swept through sleeping neighborhoods, flattened homes, and left scores dead.

Officials and rescue workers said the disaster struck at about **2:00 a.m. local time** after heavy overnight rain battered the area around **Situ Gintung**, a man-made lake in **Cirendeu, Tangerang**, near the Indonesian capital. The sudden collapse released a surge of water through densely populated residential districts below the dam.

Authorities initially reported dozens of fatalities, but the toll climbed rapidly through the day as search teams pulled bodies from mud, debris, and collapsed houses. By later counts, **around 100 people were confirmed dead**, with many others injured and some still missing. Hundreds of homes were damaged or destroyed, and thousands of residents were displaced.

## Wall of Water Hits Sleeping Residents

Survivors described waking to a roaring sound moments before floodwater smashed into their homes. Many residents had little or no warning.

Local witnesses told Indonesian media that the flood arrived as a sudden “wall of water,” tearing through narrow lanes and carrying away cars, furniture, trees, and parts of houses. Some residents climbed onto rooftops or clung to trees to survive, while others were swept away in the darkness.

One survivor was quoted by local reporters as saying the water came “very fast,” giving families only seconds to run. Another described hearing screams as neighbors tried to escape the rushing current.

The force of the flood carved through the community below the dam, leaving homes buried in thick mud and debris. In several places, only rooftops or concrete foundations remained visible after the water receded.

## Rescue Efforts Underway

Indonesian police, soldiers, disaster-response teams, and volunteers rushed to the area shortly after daybreak. Rescuers used rubber boats, ropes, and heavy equipment to search submerged houses and piles of debris.

Emergency workers carried injured residents to ambulances and temporary medical posts, while survivors gathered at mosques, schools, and government shelters. Families searched frantically for missing relatives, posting names and asking rescue teams for updates.

The search was complicated by unstable wreckage, deep mud, and clogged waterways filled with timber, household items, and vehicles. Officials warned that the death toll could rise as crews reached more damaged homes.

President **Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono** visited the scene and ordered emergency assistance for survivors. Government officials said food, clean water, blankets, and medical supplies were being sent to evacuation centers.

## Dam Failure After Heavy Rain

Situ Gintung was built during the Dutch colonial period and had long served as a reservoir and recreational lake. The dam’s failure followed intense rainfall that reportedly caused the water level to rise sharply.

Residents had previously expressed concern about the condition of the embankment, according to local accounts. After the collapse, officials said an investigation would examine whether the dam had been properly maintained and whether warnings were missed.

The breach sent an estimated large volume of reservoir water rushing downhill into neighborhoods that had expanded close to the lake over the years. The disaster highlighted the danger posed by aging infrastructure in rapidly urbanizing areas around Jakarta.

## Jakarta’s Long History of Flooding

The disaster occurred in a region already highly vulnerable to flooding. Jakarta and its surrounding metropolitan area sit on low-lying coastal land crossed by numerous rivers and drainage canals. Seasonal monsoon rains regularly overwhelm drainage systems, especially where urban development has reduced natural water absorption.

Major floods have repeatedly hit the capital, including severe flooding in **2007**, when large parts of Jakarta were submerged and dozens of people were killed. Contributing factors include:

- Heavy monsoon rainfall  
- Poor drainage and clogged canals  
- Rapid urban growth in flood-prone areas  
- Deforestation and development upstream  
- Land subsidence caused partly by groundwater extraction  
- Aging flood-control infrastructure  

While the Situ Gintung disaster was caused by a dam breach rather than ordinary river flooding, experts said it underscored the broader risks facing communities around Jakarta: dense settlement, weak infrastructure oversight, and exposure to extreme rainfall.

## Families Await News

As night fell, rescue teams continued searching the devastated area. Survivors stood amid mud-covered streets, trying to recover belongings from wrecked homes. Many said they had lost everything within minutes.

Officials said the priority remained finding the missing, treating the injured, and providing shelter for displaced families. An investigation into the cause of the dam collapse was expected to begin once emergency operations were complete.

The Situ Gintung dam disaster is now remembered as one of the deadliest flood-related tragedies in Indonesia’s recent history.

# Before Dawn, a Wall of Water: Cirendeu Flash Flood Kills Dozens After Dam Failure Near Jakarta

**CIRENDEU, Indonesia** — A catastrophic flash flood tore through the Cirendeu area on the southwestern edge of Jakarta before dawn after an aging dam holding back a lake burst, sending a wall of water into sleeping neighborhoods and leaving dozens dead, hundreds displaced, and entire streets buried in mud and debris.

The disaster struck in the early hours, when most residents were still asleep. Within minutes, water from the breached dam surged downhill through densely populated settlements, smashing through homes, overturning vehicles, and sweeping away families who had little or no warning.

Local officials said the flood was triggered by the failure of the embankment at **Situ Gintung**, a reservoir in the Cirendeu area, following heavy rain. The lake, long used for water storage and recreation, sits above residential neighborhoods that grew increasingly crowded over the years.

“This happened very quickly,” one emergency official said at the scene. “The water came down with tremendous force, and many people were caught inside their homes.”

## Homes Swept Away Before Sunrise

Residents described waking to a roar in the darkness, followed by water crashing through doors and windows.

“I heard a sound like thunder, then the water came,” said one survivor, standing near the remains of a damaged house. “There was no time to save anything. We just ran.”

Another resident said the flood felt like “a small tsunami,” with waves carrying trees, household furniture, motorcycles, and pieces of buildings through narrow lanes.

“I was sleeping when my neighbors shouted that the dam had broken,” he said. “When I opened the door, the water was already at my chest.”

By sunrise, the scale of the destruction was visible: collapsed brick walls, roofs torn from houses, mud-covered roads, and dazed survivors searching for relatives. Rescue workers pulled bodies from wreckage while volunteers helped evacuate the injured and elderly.

## Dozens Killed, Many Missing

Authorities reported dozens of deaths, with the number expected to rise as rescue teams continued searching through mud-filled homes and debris. Many victims were believed to have drowned after being trapped indoors or swept away in the first rush of water.

Hospitals and emergency posts received survivors suffering from broken bones, cuts, shock, and hypothermia. Temporary shelters were set up in schools, mosques, and public buildings for residents who lost their homes.

“We are still searching,” a rescue coordinator said. “Some houses were completely destroyed, and the mud is very thick. It is difficult work.”

Officials said hundreds of people had been forced from their homes. Many survivors escaped with only the clothes they were wearing.

“My house is gone,” said a mother looking for relatives at an evacuation center. “Everything is gone — our clothes, our documents, our savings. I don’t know where we will sleep next.”

## Questions Over Dam Safety

The collapse raised immediate questions about the condition of the dam and whether warnings had been ignored. Residents said they had worried for years about cracks, leaks, and poor maintenance around the reservoir embankment.

“We knew the dam was old,” one community member said. “People talked about it, especially after heavy rain. But nobody thought it would break like this.”

Officials acknowledged that the structure would be investigated.

“We need to know why the embankment failed,” a local government representative said. “If there was negligence, it must be addressed. But right now our priority is evacuation, medical care, and finding the missing.”

Disaster specialists noted that rapid urban growth around Jakarta has placed many low-lying and downstream communities at increasing risk. Informal housing, poor drainage, deforestation, and aging infrastructure can turn heavy rainfall into deadly floods.

## Rescue Effort Underway

Search-and-rescue teams, police, soldiers, medical workers, and volunteers converged on the area throughout the day. Heavy equipment was brought in to clear debris, though narrow roads and unstable ground slowed the operation.

At evacuation centers, families waited anxiously for news of missing loved ones. Lists of survivors and victims were posted as officials tried to identify the dead.

President and senior government officials were expected to review the damage and coordinate emergency support. Aid agencies delivered food, clean water, blankets, medicine, and clothing.

“We ask people to remain calm and follow instructions from rescue teams,” an official said. “The area is still dangerous.”

## A Community in Shock

For many residents of Cirendeu, the flood transformed a familiar neighborhood into a disaster zone in a matter of minutes.

Children sat wrapped in donated blankets while adults tried to salvage belongings from the mud. Some searched for identity cards and school books; others dug through broken concrete and timber, hoping to find missing relatives.

“I lost my neighbor, my friend,” one survivor said quietly. “Last night we were talking. This morning, his house was gone.”

As night fell after the disaster, the immediate emergency remained unresolved. Rescue teams continued searching, survivors crowded into shelters, and officials faced urgent questions about how an aging dam above a crowded neighborhood could fail so suddenly — and why so many people had been left in its path.
